extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, newsroom staff, media-watch readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards about originality, attribution, investigation, correction, and consequences when news stories reproduce material published elsewhere. Focused on newsroom practices for identifying and handling plagiarism in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: WIRED's journalistic standards (originality)
rubrics_metrics.description: THIS STORY DOES not meet WIRED’s journalistic standards as it reproduces material published elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality is required; reproducing material published elsewhere violates the outlet's standards. When material is found to reproduce other sources without proper attribution, it is considered a breach of journalistic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and linking to original sources
rubrics_metrics.description: A freelance journalist contacted editors 'just asking for a link back in the future' — implying proper practice is to credit/source original reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using material derived from others' reporting, provide clear attribution and links back to the original. If a creator requests credit or a link, editors should consider honoring that and ensure future stories properly cite sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to external tips and promptly investigate suspect copy
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor received a direct message about potential plagiarism, thanked the tipster, and reviewed the material more closely when arriving at the desk roughly 45 minutes later; that investigation uncovered problems in multiple stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms should take external allegations seriously, acknowledge tipsters, and investigate promptly. Patterns across multiple pieces should trigger broader review of an author's body of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial transparency: label content that fails standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Each affected story was tagged with an editor's note explaining it did not meet WIRED's journalistic standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a story is found to fall short of standards, publishers should add clear editor's notes explaining the issue to readers rather than silently removing content. Such notes should state the nature of the breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve public/archival record even when standards are breached
rubrics_metrics.description: WIRED chose to keep the problematic stories online 'for archival purposes and the public record.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than wholesale deletion, outlets may retain problematic content with explanatory notes to preserve the public record and allow readers to see corrections and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious consequences for patterns of plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Nic Cavell was fired after editors uncovered a pattern of plagiarism across four stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated or systematic plagiarism can lead to termination or other serious employment consequences. Enforcement of policies should be proportional to the scale and pattern of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical cases to inform vigilance and response
rubrics_metrics.description: The article references a prior incident (Jonah Lehrer in 2012) where multiple posts had problems ranging from plagiarism to factual issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms should learn from past incidents of misconduct to strengthen detection, review processes, and editorial standards, and to recognize warning signs in contributors' work.
